text.t: Lysozyme is a small enzyme, one chain of 129 amino acids, from hen egg white.
Its job is to break open the cell walls of bacteria.
Look for a long cleft across the surface: this is the active site where the sugar chain of a bacterial cell wall binds.
Glutamate 35 and aspartate 52 are the enzyme's two active-site amino acids.
They sit in the long cleft where the enzyme cuts the sugar chain of the bacterial cell wall.
Four disulfide bridges staple the chain to itself in this small, stable enzyme.
Hen egg-white lysozyme was the first enzyme ever to have its structure solved.

does.t: Lysozyme attacks the carbohydrate chains that brace a bacterium's cell wall.
Once those chains are cut, the bacterium bursts under its own internal pressure.
Our tears and mucus contain lysozyme to protect exposed surfaces from infection.

shape.t: A long groove in the enzyme holds a stretch of the bacterial sugar chain so it can be cut.
Computer models suggested lysozyme bends one sugar ring out of its usual shape to make it easier to break, though other studies point to electric charges as more important.

text.t: Lysozyme is found in egg white, where it guards the food stored for the growing chick, and in our tears, mucus and blood.
Its target is the bacterial cell wall.
This file is a 1974 refinement of the hen egg-white lysozyme structure at 2.0 angstroms.
Alexander Fleming discovered lysozyme by chance when a drop of mucus from his cold killed bacteria in a dish.

compare.t: Lysozyme measures about 4.9 nm from end to end.
That makes it smaller than hemoglobin in this gallery, which measures about 7 nm.

text.t: One of the two active-site amino acids.
